analysis.one_liner: Funds the removal of lead pipes and taps from homes, paid for by closing the carried-interest tax break and raising the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The GET THE LEAD OUT Act was introduced in the House on July 22, 2026 and referred to three committees; it has one cosponsor and no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would spend up to $9.5 billion a year, for ten years, on finding and removing lead pipes and taps from homes, with priority on low-income housing. It would also require landlords and home sellers to disclose lead pipe hazards, set training and certification rules for contractors who do the removal work, and expand what federally assisted housing programs can pay for. To cover the cost, it would tax investment fund managers' 'carried interest' as ordinary income and roll the estate and gift tax exemption back to its pre-2018 level.
analysis.who_benefits: Families living in older homes with lead plumbing, especially low-income renters and children under 6, who face risks of permanent neurological damage from lead in their drinking water. State and local governments get grant money to test and remove lead hazards, and certified contractors get a new stream of funded abatement work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters and children in older housing

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $9.5 billion per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2035 in HUD grants for evaluating and removing lead-based pipe hazards in affordable housing, including testing children's blood-lead levels afterward.
Requires risk assessments and lead hazard reduction in federally assisted housing, with at least half of units assessed within five years of enactment and the rest within ten years.

Requires sellers and landlords to disclose known lead pipes and hazards before a sale or lease, gives buyers a 10-day window to test for lead, and imposes civil penalties and triple damages on those who knowingly violate the disclosure rules.
Creates EPA certification and training standards so that lead pipe inspections and abatement are performed only by certified contractors.
Lets HUD, HOME, and Community Development Block Grant funds be spent on lead pipe hazard reduction, and lets Section 8 rents be adjusted to cover removal costs.

analysis.who_pays: Investment fund managers, whose carried-interest profits would be taxed as ordinary income rather than at lower capital gains rates, and very large estates, which would lose the higher post-2017 estate and gift tax exemption. Landlords and sellers of pre-1986 homes also bear new testing, disclosure, and abatement obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fund managers, large estates, some landlords

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates risk assessments, abatement, and disclosure across federally assisted and pre-1986 housing; landlords and sellers facing those costs may pass them to tenants and buyers through rents and prices.

The revenue provisions hit private investment partnerships and large estates, and critics of carried-interest changes argue that taxing manager profits as ordinary income raises the cost of investment; the bill's own task force acknowledges uncertainty around liability and financing for lead removal in rental housing.

The bill is referred to three committees at once (Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, and Ways and Means), a path that typically slows a bill by splitting jurisdiction, and it authorizes spending that still requires separate annual appropriations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Removing lead from drinking water addresses a proven cause of permanent harm to children, and the bill directs the cost at very wealthy households and a narrow tax benefit for fund managers. The offsets are narrowly drawn (they target investment managers, not all wealthy households) and the landlord mandates could raise costs for some renters, but the core trade — lead removal versus carried interest and estate-tax breaks — favors ordinary households if the money is actually appropriated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to three House committees, and as of the latest record none of them has taken it up, so it is waiting and may simply expire at the end of the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Shontel Brown introduced the GET THE LEAD OUT Act of 2026 in the House on July 22, 2026, joined by Rep. Rashida Tlaib as its one cosponsor.
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Financial Services and Ways and Means Committees.
No hearings, markups, votes, or further actions appear in the action history after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved: lead remains in the affected housing, and investment managers and large estates keep the current tax treatment. If the bill never advances, the status quo is who comes out ahead.

for.name: Rep. Shontel Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to three committees.

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats are on the bill so far and no roll-call votes have occurred, so the partisan split is not yet established.

industries.industry: Private equity and investment fund managers
industries.note: The bill taxes 'carried interest' — the manager's share of investment fund profits — as ordinary income and treats gains from selling these partnership interests as ordinary income, ending a lower-taxed break. This raises taxes on a small group of very high earners to fund the lead removal program.
Rolling the estate and gift tax basic exclusion back to its pre-2018 amount means large estates lose part of the shelter from estate tax that they have held since 2018.
The bill channels roughly $9.5 billion a year into inspections and pipe removal, and requires certified contractors, creating a funded market for trained abatement firms and workers.

industries.industry: Landlords and sellers of pre-1986 homes
industries.note: They face new disclosure, inspection, and abatement obligations with penalties for knowingly hiding lead hazards, but the bill also directs a task force to explore liability 'safe harbors,' insurance availability, and financing to offset those costs.
The bill requires EPA certification standards for labs testing water, pipes, and taps for lead, and mandated risk assessments create steady demand for accredited testing.

analysis.trajectory: A bill with two cosponsors referred to three committees rarely gets a hearing, markup, or floor vote in the roughly five months left in this Congress; unless it attracts broad support or moves as part of a larger package, it will likely expire when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
